article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Indica
Genetics: Afghan cannabis × Northern Light
Breeder: Sagarmatha Seeds
THC Content: 20%
CBD Content: N/A
Terpene Profile: N/A
Primary Flavors: Earth, hash, pine, wood, musk, herbs
Flowering Time (Indoor): 55–60 days
Outdoor Harvest Time: October
Indoor Yield: 300–325 g/m²
Outdoor Yield: Moderate
Grow Difficulty: Easy to intermediate

Slyder was built around a single uncompromising idea: take the kind of deeply sedating Afghan cannabis traditionally associated with hash-producing regions and make it practical for an indoor Dutch garden. Sagarmatha Seeds traces the cultivar to seeds obtained in Afghanistan, later crossed with a potent Northern Light so the line would perform more reliably under artificial lighting. The finished plant stayed true to its indica roots—short, dark, resinous, and physically heavy—but gained the compact structure and predictable flowering behavior needed for indoor production. Sagarmatha still describes Slyder as a one-meter plant finishing in roughly 55–60 days with 300–325 grams per square meter of dried flower.

Even the name comes from the effect rather than the aroma or appearance. The breeder’s old description jokes that consumers may feel so much weight in their feet that they “slide” them instead of lifting them while moving around the house. Beneath the humor is a fairly precise description of the experience: this is not marijuana bred for productivity, social energy, or complicated flavor chasing. Slyder is classic heavy indica weed—compact, resin-rich, hash-oriented, and deliberately suited to the end of the day.
Genetics and Lineage

Sagarmatha’s own breeder description identifies Slyder as Afghan cannabis crossed with Northern Light. The Afghan side came from seeds obtained in Afghanistan, while the Northern Light parent was added specifically to make those traditional genetics more suitable for indoor cultivation. The breeder does not identify the Northern Light as a numbered selection such as #5 or #9, so attaching a specific number to the parent would go beyond the documented lineage.

A historical account published in Ed Rosenthal ’s The Big Book of Buds Vol. 2 adds context to the Afghan material. It describes an Amsterdam cannabis traveler obtaining seeds from farmers in the Afghanistan/Khyber Pass region after the Soviet withdrawal and selecting material noted for powerful sedative qualities. The book then explains that those Afghan plants were poorly adapted to Dutch indoor conditions until they were crossed with Northern Lights, producing the compact indoor-oriented Slyder.

Genetically, that pairing makes sense. Afghan cannabis populations are closely associated with squat plants, thick foliage, dense resin coverage, hash production, and strong body-centered effects. Northern Light became famous for many of the same practical traits while also proving highly effective under indoor cultivation. Slyder therefore represents reinforcement rather than contrast: two indica-oriented gene pools combined to emphasize compact size, resin, rapid flowering, and deep physical relaxation.
Effects and Experience

Slyder does not hide its purpose behind a long cerebral introduction. The effect builds heavily through the body, often creating a sensation of physical weight before the consumer realizes how far the experience has progressed. Sagarmatha calls the stone strong and lethargic and specifically describes it as producing an almost imagined paralysis or heaviness in the feet. The breeder’s current guidance still labels the high as extremely relaxing and especially appropriate before sleep.

Mental activity tends to soften along with the body. Thoughts may become slower, concentration less urgent, and simple entertainment increasingly satisfying. This is the sort of cannabis that fits a quiet night at home much better than errands, detailed work, exercise, or social situations requiring sharp attention. Moderate amounts may feel warm and tranquil; larger amounts can push the experience toward couch-lock and sleep.

No defensible original THC percentage should be assigned to the cultivar. Slyder comes from a period when seed catalogs were more likely to describe effect and plant performance than publish standardized cannabinoid testing. Modern examples can vary substantially by phenotype, cultivation, harvest timing, and laboratory methodology. Consumers should rely on current batch testing when available, because even old-school indica weed can produce pronounced impairment, dizziness, anxiety, short-term memory disruption, or excessive sedation.
Medical Benefits

The cultivar’s profoundly relaxing character explains why it has often been discussed in connection with nighttime medical marijuana use. Some patients may find a heavy body effect desirable when dealing with chronic discomfort, muscle tension, or difficulty sleeping. That historical reputation, however, is not evidence that Slyder itself treats pain, insomnia, or another medical condition. No controlled clinical trial has evaluated the named strain.

Cannabis research more broadly provides a limited framework for understanding those uses. The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health notes that cannabis and cannabinoid products may provide modest benefit for some forms of chronic pain. Studies involving sleep have sometimes shown better sleep quality or shorter time to sleep among people with other health conditions, although it remains unclear whether cannabinoids directly improve sleep or whether patients sleep better because another symptom improves.

That uncertainty matters with a cultivar as sedating as Slyder. Sleepiness can be desirable in one context and a serious impairment in another. THC-containing cannabis may also cause dizziness, altered judgment, attention problems, anxiety, or medication interactions. Medical use should therefore depend on current cannabinoid testing, conservative dosing, and appropriate healthcare guidance rather than the strain’s heavy reputation alone.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Slyder’s aromatic identity belongs firmly to the old Afghan-indica tradition. Earth, dried herbs, wood, musk, and resin form the base, while pine and a mild sweetness can emerge as the flowers are broken apart. The character is closer to traditional hash and dried plant spice than to modern candy, cream, or tropical fruit cultivars.

The breeder creates an interesting distinction between flower aroma and grow-room discretion. Sagarmatha describes the mature buds as strongly aromatic while also praising the variety for relatively low odor during indoor production. That combination suggests a plant whose smell intensifies considerably after handling and curing rather than constantly filling the room during every stage of growth.

No breeder-issued terpene chromatography panel exists for the original release, so claims of fixed myrcene, beta-caryophyllene, pinene, or other terpene percentages should be treated cautiously. Those compounds would fit the earthy, woody, spicy, and pine-like sensory profile, but the historical record supports the aroma itself more strongly than any exact chemical ranking. A careful dry and cure will preserve more of the subtle herbal and resinous complexity that can be lost if dense flowers are dried too quickly.
Growing Information

Indoor cultivation is where Slyder was deliberately designed to excel. Sagarmatha recommends allowing plants to develop approximately four to seven internodes before clipping the center cola. That topping strategy encourages branching and helps convert the naturally dominant Afghan-style main stem into a wider productive canopy. The breeder lists average finished height at around one meter, making the cultivar manageable in spaces where taller sativas would become impractical.

Sea of Green is particularly well suited to the plant. Historical cultivation material describes Slyder performing effectively either as a multi-branched specimen or in SOG, where compact plants can fill an indoor canopy efficiently. Yield is listed at approximately 300–325 grams per square meter of dried flower, with flowering taking around 55–60 days. The Big Book of Buds account likewise describes mature plants as compact, conifer-shaped specimens with dark olive foliage and dense resinous flowers.

The flowers themselves can become dense enough that humidity management deserves attention. Afghan-dominant weed often produces thick floral clusters with substantial internal mass, so good air movement remains important even when plants appear healthy externally. Removing excessive interior foliage and avoiding prolonged late-flower humidity can help reduce the risk of botrytis developing inside dense colas.

Nutrition should remain measured rather than excessive. Compact indica plants can appear extremely sturdy, but overfeeding can still burn leaf tips or interfere with normal ripening. A steady program that follows plant response is preferable to pushing nutrients simply because the cultivar is capable of carrying heavy resinous flowers.

Sagarmatha does not publish an official outdoor harvest date or outdoor yield for Slyder. The genetics can be cultivated outdoors, but the original breeding project was specifically aimed at adapting Afghan material to indoor Dutch conditions. Growers working outside should therefore treat climate, latitude, flowering initiation, and local autumn weather as more useful guides than unsupported calendar dates repeated on secondary databases.

Harvest quality is closely tied to maturity. Because the cultivar was selected for powerful sedation and resin, allowing flowers to reach full trichome development is central to preserving its intended character. A slow dry followed by several weeks of curing can deepen the earthy-hash aroma while smoothing the sharper herbal and woody notes.
FAQ
What strain is Slyder?

Slyder is an indica bred by Sagarmatha Seeds from Afghan cannabis genetics crossed with a potent Northern Light. The cross was specifically created to adapt the Afghan material to reliable indoor cultivation.
Who bred Slyder?

Sagarmatha Seeds bred the cultivar. The Amsterdam breeder has operated for decades, with current company information identifying Tony Rhodes as its principal geneticist and describing a long history working with Dutch and American cannabis genetics.
How long does Slyder take to flower?
Sagarmatha Seeds lists an indoor flowering period of approximately 55–60 days. The breeder recommends vegetating plants until four to seven internodes have formed and then clipping the center cola.
What does Slyder taste like?

The profile is classic old-school indica: earthy, hash-like, woody, musky, herbal, and piney, with mild sweetness underneath. There is no official original terpene analysis assigning exact percentages to individual compounds.
Is Slyder good for nighttime use?

Sagarmatha specifically characterizes the effect as extremely relaxing and ideal before sleep. The strain’s heavy body stone and lethargic progression make it much better suited to late-day or nighttime use than situations requiring sustained concentration or physical coordination.
Final Thoughts on Slyder

Slyder is one of those marijuana strains whose identity becomes clearer the less modern marketing language is applied to it. Sagarmatha did not create it to taste like pastry, test at an eye-catching THC percentage, or produce a highly energetic hybrid effect. The breeding objective was simpler and more practical: preserve the profoundly sedating character of Afghan cannabis while making the plant dependable indoors.

Northern Light provided the bridge. By crossing the Afghan material with an indoor-proven indica, Sagarmatha produced a compact plant averaging about one meter tall, finishing in 55–60 days, and yielding roughly 300–325 grams per square meter. The breeder’s recommended topping method and the cultivar’s compatibility with Sea of Green further underline how strongly indoor production shaped the project.

What reaches the consumer remains unmistakably traditional. Earth, hash, pine, musk, wood, and herbs surround dense resinous flowers, while the high settles quickly into the body and can progress toward profound lethargy and sleep. That heavy physical effect is so central to the cultivar that it inspired the name itself.
